description: Agency Protocol Standard semantic review, content-level exposure corrections, retired-ID cleanup and verified narrow retest-history retry correction. Trial by Graph remains disabled. No private assessment material.

fields.q: Why can a risk-averse buyer and an insurer both gain from coverage?
options: The buyer values reduced uncertainty and the insurer can pool and bear financial risk
Both receive higher expected cash payouts than they contribute
The premium makes the physical loss event less likely by itself
Pooling removes the insurer’s expected claim cost
fields.feedback: Risk transfer can create value beyond expected cash returns; claims and premiums remain real.

fields.q: A customer values coverage at $250, while expected claims plus administration cost the insurer $180. At a $220 premium, which gains arise?
options: Buyer surplus $30 and insurer expected profit $40
Buyer surplus $70 and insurer expected profit $40
Buyer surplus $30 and insurer expected profit $70
Buyer surplus −$40 and insurer expected profit $40
fields.feedback: Buyer surplus is 250−220=30; insurer expected profit is 220−180=40. Risk aversion explains willingness to pay.

fields.q: An insurer covers shops in one flood zone. More policies add mostly correlated claims. A manager claims that doubling the policy count doubles diversification. What is the best evaluation?
options: Count alone is insufficient; compare correlation and the cost of adding independent exposures
The claim holds because equal premiums make losses independent
The claim holds whenever each policy’s expected loss is unchanged
Diversification is irrelevant whenever buyers are risk averse
fields.feedback: Pooling depends on dependence across losses, not just count. Independent exposures may improve risk bearing, but their acquisition costs also matter.

fields.q: An insurer cannot distinguish applicants’ risk, and higher-risk applicants disproportionately enroll at a pooled premium. What is this?
options: Adverse selection
Moral hazard from changed precautions
Favorable selection
Screening that has revealed every type
fields.feedback: Hidden risk changes the composition of enrollees toward higher expected cost. No change in care is specified.

fields.q: A plan’s optional preventive-service package appeals most to customers who already have low expected claims. Those customers enroll disproportionately, with no change in their behavior. What does this show?
options: Favorable selection of lower-cost participants
Adverse selection of higher-cost participants
Moral hazard caused by reduced precautions
A treatment effect proving insurance made customers safer
fields.feedback: Lower-cost types are more likely to participate before any behavior change. This is favorable selection rather than causal prevention.

fields.q: At a pooled premium, low-risk buyers leave and high-risk buyers remain. No one changes care. Management proposes only more inspections of current precautions. What is missing?
options: A response to enrollment composition; care inspections alone do not establish better risk selection
Proof that each customer’s risk rose after coverage
A reason to reduce all premiums regardless of the remaining pool’s claims
A way to hide risk categories so the same premium appears fair
fields.feedback: The pool deteriorated through selection. Information or contract design must address who enrolls; current care is a different margin.

fields.q: A firm requires applicants to perform a work sample before hiring. Who is screening whom?
options: The less-informed firm screens applicants’ ability
Applicants screen the firm’s quality through their work
Applicants independently signal through a credential they designed
The firm monitors effort on work after employment begins
fields.feedback: The firm initiates the test to obtain private ability information before hiring.

fields.q: An insurer offers a low-premium high-deductible policy and a higher-premium full-coverage policy. Risk types choose differently even with care fixed. Which mechanism is at work?
options: Screening through a menu designed by the insurer
Monitoring of precautions after policy purchase
Signaling initiated independently by customers
Risk pooling that makes each type’s claims identical
fields.feedback: The insurer uses self-selection to learn risk. A deductible can screen types as well as affect care in other contexts.

fields.q: A work-sample test costs $4,000 and avoids expected hiring mistakes worth $15,000, but delays hiring enough to lose $6,000 of output. It does not observe later effort. Which conclusion follows?
options: Net gain is $5,000; later effort still needs suitable incentives or monitoring
Net gain is $11,000; hiring delay is not a screening cost
Net gain is $15,000; screening costs are internal transfers
Net gain is $5,000; passing removes later hidden-effort problems
fields.feedback: Selection gains net 15−4−6=5 thousand. Better selection does not ensure effort after hiring.

fields.q: A supplier independently obtains a credible quality certificate before bidding. What makes this signaling?
options: The informed supplier chooses evidence that reveals its quality
The buyer requires every bidder to take its own test
The certificate observes effort after the job is completed
The supplier changes buyers’ financial exposure to every loss
fields.feedback: The informed party initiates the information-revealing action. Credibility matters; a bare claim need not separate types.

fields.q: A credential brings a $20 reward. It costs high-ability applicants $6 and low-ability applicants $28. Assuming payoff maximization, who obtains it?
options: High-ability applicants only
Both types because the reward is positive
Low-ability applicants only
Neither type because obtaining it has a cost
fields.feedback: Net rewards are 14 and −8, so only high-ability applicants choose the credential.

fields.q: An enforceable warranty separates seller types because poor-quality sellers face more claims. A loophole now lets every seller deny claims cheaply. Which conclusion follows?
options: The commitment may stop separating types; enforcement must restore meaningful type-dependent cost
It becomes stronger because all sellers can offer a cheaper warranty
It becomes buyer screening merely because buyers read the warranty
It still reveals quality whenever its printed coverage is generous
fields.feedback: The signal depends on a credible differential commitment. If poor-quality sellers can imitate cheaply, the written promise alone is insufficient.

fields.q: How do verified seller histories help a new buyer?
options: They provide imperfect evidence of reliability before the buyer chooses
They directly observe every action on the buyer’s future order
They transfer the buyer’s financial loss to a third party
They reveal the buyer’s private willingness to pay to all sellers
fields.feedback: Past performance can inform a future selection decision without making quality certain.

fields.q: A platform finds repeated verified evidence of seller misrepresentation and removes those sellers. Which effect targets adverse selection?
options: The remaining pool can contain fewer unreliable sellers
Each remaining buyer receives full insurance against every loss
Every remaining seller’s future effort becomes directly observable
The platform learns each buyer’s willingness to pay
fields.feedback: Evidence-based exclusion changes seller composition. It does not guarantee perfect quality or observe all future actions.

fields.q: A marketplace wants credible ratings, but reliable newcomers have no history and some established sellers buy fake reviews. Which design best addresses both problems?
options: Verify reviews and offer newcomers independent quality checks, weighing their costs
Exclude every newcomer indefinitely and count all existing reviews equally
Accept anonymous reviews as sufficient because a larger sample removes manipulation
Replace ratings with deposits and assume any deposit proves quality
fields.feedback: Authenticity checks address fake evidence; an alternative verification path reduces exclusion of reliable entrants. Both costs and credibility must be assessed.

fields.q: A covered customer secretly reduces precautions because others now bear much of the loss. Which problem is present?
options: Moral hazard from hidden action
Adverse selection from pre-existing type
Favorable selection from lower-risk entry
Screening initiated by the insurer
fields.feedback: Coverage changes the payoff from care; hidden action is distinct from who originally enrolled.

fields.q: A policy screens risk before enrollment but reimburses every loss afterward. Care is unobservable and precautions fall. Which addition targets that remaining margin?
options: Loss sharing or verifiable precaution incentives
A second ability test that leaves care payoffs unchanged
A rule ignoring all post-enrollment choices
A premium label change with identical payments and coverage
fields.feedback: Entry information does not itself preserve care. The remedy must affect actions or their observability.

fields.q: Before offering full reimbursement of employees’ expenses, what question anticipates moral hazard?
options: How will employees’ spending choices change when they bear less of the cost?
Which applicants had high expenses before being hired?
Which credentials credibly revealed employee ability before hiring?
How many employees prefer insurance against uncertain household losses?
fields.feedback: Anticipation concerns behavior under the reimbursement incentive, even though the question is asked before contracting.

fields.q: An insured buyer skips useful precautions because losses are fully reimbursed. How does a deductible address this?
options: It raises the buyer’s personal loss from an accident
It directly reveals every precaution to the insurer
It proves the buyer was low-risk before enrollment
It makes physical loss events independent across customers
fields.feedback: Loss sharing changes the payoff from care without directly observing it.

fields.q: A deductible prevents $30 of expected avoidable loss but sacrifices $22 in valued protection. Inspection prevents $24 and costs $10. The reforms are mutually exclusive; other effects are equal. Which is better?
options: Inspection: net $14 versus $8 for the deductible
Deductible: $30 prevented loss exceeds $24
Deductible: lost protection is not an economic cost
Inspection: net $24 because inspection costs are internal
fields.feedback: Compare 24−10=14 with 30−22=8. Care incentives must be weighed against the value of insurance.

fields.q: How does monitoring address hidden action?
options: It makes conduct or relevant evidence more observable
It changes pay solely by raising the fixed salary
It identifies only ability before a relationship begins
It shifts all financial uncertainty to an insurer
fields.feedback: Observation or verification reduces uncertainty about behavior; it differs from pay design and entry screening.

fields.q: A delivery firm observes location data but not whether parcels reach customers. Drivers meet location targets while leaving parcels undelivered. Which improvement fits?
options: Verify actual delivery rather than reward location data alone
Raise pay per recorded location without checking delivery
Retest pre-hire driving ability while keeping delivery measures unchanged
Infer completed delivery whenever a vehicle reaches the correct street
fields.feedback: The observed proxy omits the principal’s actual delivery objective. Verification should target that outcome.

fields.q: Checking every expense claim costs $18,000 and prevents $24,000 of abuse. Targeted audits cost $7,000 and prevent $18,000. Other effects equal, which choice follows?
options: Targeted audits net $11,000 versus $6,000 for full checking
Full checking wins because $24,000 exceeds $18,000
Targeted audits net $18,000 because audit expense is not a loss
Full checking removes the need for any future incentives
fields.feedback: Control value is prevention minus cost: 18−7=11 and 24−18=6 thousand. Maximum surveillance need not be optimal.

fields.q: An employee deliberately supplies less required effort when that effort is hard to observe. What is this?
options: Shirking
Hidden ability at hiring
An honest output loss from an external shock
Voluntary signaling before hiring
fields.feedback: Shirking concerns hidden effort during work, not every poor result or low pre-hire ability.

fields.q: A team bonus is shared equally. One worker’s effort is hidden and raises total output, but adds little to that worker’s own pay. What is the main incentive concern?
options: The worker may free ride because private reward understates the effort’s joint benefit
The bonus directly reveals every member’s effort
Equal pay proves that all workers have equal ability
Higher team output proves no member can reduce effort
fields.feedback: Equal sharing can dilute the individual payoff from effort even when the team benefits.

fields.q: Individual-output bonuses raise measured output but reduce needed teamwork. Close surveillance would reveal teamwork but is costly. Which response fits both facts?
options: Compare team-relevant rewards and selective verification, counting measurement cost and individual free riding
Raise individual-output bonuses and omit teamwork from evaluation
Pay only a team bonus and assume individual effort becomes observable
Monitor every action without counting the resources used
fields.feedback: The remedy must recognize both task substitution and free riding. Better measures and verification help only if their value exceeds their costs.

fields.q: After funds are issued, a borrower secretly shifts into a riskier project that transfers expected losses to the bank. Which problem is this?
options: Lending moral hazard
Only pre-loan adverse selection
Screening initiated by the borrower
Signaling that proves the project is safe
fields.feedback: The relevant private choice occurs after funding under an incentive to shift losses.

fields.q: A borrower can choose project risk after funding. Why may pledged collateral strengthen care?
options: Default puts the borrower’s own asset at risk
The pledge directly reveals each project decision
The pledge makes repayment optional in successful states
The collateral removes the borrower’s exposure to failure
fields.feedback: Collateral changes downside exposure; it is not direct observation of behavior and need not fully align risk preferences.

fields.q: A bank screens applicants accurately. Borrowers still switch secretly to risky projects after funding, and collateral is too small to offset their private upside. Which response fits?
options: Evaluate enforceable project covenants, monitoring and suitable loss exposure
Improve only the original credit score and leave later project choices unchanged
Raise promised interest and assume every borrower then chooses lower risk
Treat accurate screening as proof that the reported project will be followed
fields.feedback: Type selection and post-loan action require different controls. Collateral can be insufficient when private upside remains large.

fields.q: An owner delegates purchasing to a manager. In that relationship, who is principal and who is agent?
options: Owner is principal; purchasing manager is agent
Manager is principal; owner is agent
Supplier is principal; owner and manager are agents
Both are principals because both can benefit from purchases
fields.feedback: The owner delegates; the manager acts on the owner’s behalf.

fields.q: A manager chooses expensive suppliers that provide private perks. The owner wants value for money and cannot see the perks. Which change targets the conflict?
options: Verify competitive bids and link evaluation to purchasing value
Reward the number of supplier meetings regardless of outcomes
Raise the purchasing budget without changing evaluation
Screen the owner’s risk preferences rather than review purchases
fields.feedback: Private benefits distort the delegated choice. Observable bid and quality comparisons help align the purchasing decision.

fields.q: Why can hidden information make an incentive conflict harder to control?
options: The principal cannot readily distinguish choices serving the agent from choices serving the principal
Delegation makes the agent’s goals identical to the principal’s
Private information necessarily means the agent was unqualified at hiring
Different goals matter only when both sides observe every action
fields.feedback: Divergent objectives become harder to control when relevant types, actions or circumstances are private.

fields.q: An insurer observes safer new applicants but reduced precautions by existing customers. Average claims do not change. What should it evaluate before declaring success?
options: Only average claims because offsetting changes cancel all incentive problems
Selection and care separately, including each reform’s risk-protection costs
Only new-applicant risk because selection determines all later care
Only current care because participation cannot change the average
fields.feedback: Improved selection can conceal worse behavior. Contract value also includes risk protection, so one aggregate is insufficient.

fields.q: A manager knows specialized input quality better than the owner but accepts supplier gifts. Centralizing purchases would remove local discretion but lose useful expertise. Which design deserves comparison?
options: Centralize every detail without collecting the manager’s quality information
Keep unrestricted authority because expertise makes incentives aligned
Retain expert recommendations with verified comparisons and independent approval of conflicts
Raise fixed pay and assume gifts no longer affect supplier choice
fields.feedback: Preserve valuable information while controlling conflicted decisions; both lost expertise and control costs matter.

fields.q: An applicant conceals inadequate ability and is hired. Later the worker reduces effort when unobserved. Which pairing fits?
options: Screening at hiring and signaling during work
Moral hazard at hiring and adverse selection during work
Two cases of adverse selection because both involve private information
Adverse selection at hiring and moral hazard during work
fields.feedback: Hidden ability affects selection; hidden effort affects conduct after hiring.

fields.q: Regional profit is low. Demand was weak, effort is hidden, and the manager privately knows both local conditions and their own effort. Which evaluation is best?
options: Treat low profit alone as proof of shirking
Use independent demand benchmarks and relevant effort evidence before redesigning incentives
Treat weak demand as proof that effort incentives do not matter
Reward raw profit more strongly without checking uncontrollable conditions
fields.feedback: Output mixes effort and circumstances. Better evidence can separate them imperfectly and guide controls without inferring guilt from a bad result.

fields.q: Before choosing a control for a delegated decision, what should the principal identify?
options: The decision maker, their information, their payoff and the intended outcome
The largest available bonus before identifying what it rewards
The strictest control before checking who holds relevant information
The cheapest measure before checking whether it tracks the objective
fields.feedback: Diagnosis precedes control: identify who decides, what they know and what motivates the decision.

fields.q: Shareholders delegate operations to a CEO who values personal perks and expansion more than net company value. What creates the conflict?
options: Delegated authority combined with different objectives
Delegation makes the CEO the principal over shareholders
Shared employment guarantees identical objectives
Company growth is necessarily the same as shareholder value
fields.feedback: The shareholders are principals; the CEO acts for them but can pursue a different payoff.

fields.q: A manager privately knows operating costs but earns bonuses on revenue alone. Which risk follows?
options: The manager may select high-revenue decisions that reduce profit
Private information automatically makes the manager’s goals match the owner’s
Revenue measurement reveals every cost the manager knows
The manager’s behavior can only be explained by pre-hire ability
fields.feedback: Private cost information and a narrow reward can support actions that serve the agent but harm the owner.

fields.q: Why are audits a cost of controlling agency conflict?
options: They use resources to make the agent’s conduct more observable
They are internal prices that only move profit between divisions
They establish that every remaining bad outcome is misconduct
They reveal only ability before the agent is selected
fields.feedback: Audits consume resources to verify behavior. Their benefit must be compared with their cost.

fields.q: An owner can verify outcomes that closely reflect effort, but continuous surveillance is costly. Which alternative may reduce surveillance needs?
options: Link some pay to those verified outcomes
Raise fixed pay without changing the return to effort
Retest entry qualifications while ignoring current output
Count employee activity without any quality verification
fields.feedback: Outcome-related pay can align effort if its measure reflects the owner’s objective. It is not costless or universally superior.

fields.q: Broad auditing prevents $90,000 of agency losses, costs $60,000 and delays valuable decisions by $20,000. A pay redesign prevents $65,000 but costs $25,000 in implementation and risk compensation. Other effects equal, which is better?
options: Pay redesign: $40,000 net versus $10,000 for broad audit
Broad audit: $90,000 prevented loss exceeds $65,000
Broad audit: $30,000 net because delay is not a monitoring invoice
Pay redesign: $65,000 net because compensation is costless to the firm
fields.feedback: Evaluate complete consequences: 65−25=40 and 90−60−20=10 thousand. The supplied sources do not require an assumed named three-part taxonomy.

fields.q: Sales staff earn revenue bonuses and discount below incremental cost to raise sales. Which metric change targets this behavior?
options: Reward verified contribution after relevant selling costs
Raise the revenue target but retain the same bonus basis
Reward number of invoices regardless of their margin
Classify all discounting as misconduct regardless of contribution
fields.feedback: Contribution includes the omitted costs; some discounts remain profitable, so the remedy should not prohibit them all.

fields.q: A service team is paid for short calls but the firm wants durable problem resolution. Staff rush customers off the line. Which change targets the diagnosed gap?
options: Reward verified resolution along with response time
Pay more for short calls while keeping the same measure
Retest applicants’ credentials without changing service rewards
Raise fixed pay and assume the marginal speed incentive disappears
fields.feedback: The reward omits service quality. Adding a relevant verified outcome addresses the actual decision incentive.

fields.q: Which behavior is gaming a performance metric?
options: Raising a score by sacrificing outcomes the principal values
Raising a score by improving the intended outcome
Missing an honest forecast after an unexpected demand shock
Reporting a defect in the measure before rewards are set
fields.feedback: Gaming exploits the measured target at the expense of its purpose; productive response is different.

fields.q: Headquarters knows cross-branch constraints; branches know current local customers. What makes decision-rights design a tradeoff?
options: Central coordination and local information can both have value
Delegating authority makes branch incentives match company profit
Central authority gives headquarters every local fact without cost
Information sharing alone determines who has decision authority
fields.feedback: Rights, information and incentives must be considered together; neither central nor local authority is universally best.

fields.q: Local volume bonuses cause branches to undercut one another. Headquarters can observe prices promptly. Why might central approval help?
options: It can internalize cross-branch effects ignored by local volume targets
It gives each branch a stronger reason to poach sister customers
It replaces the need to know costs when setting prices
It makes local customer information irrelevant to every price
fields.feedback: Central review can coordinate spillovers when relevant information is available; delay and local information remain costs to assess.

fields.q: Central price approval stops unprofitable discounts but loses urgent high-margin orders. Branches know customer timing. Which comparison should headquarters make next?
options: Compare central approval with margin-based local authority and targeted review, including delay and control costs
Retain central approval because any gain over the old system proves optimality
Restore volume-only bonuses because any delay proves delegation is better
Delegate every shared decision without sending branches capacity information
fields.feedback: A hybrid can preserve speed while controlling the original metric conflict. Evaluate both information and incentive consequences.

fields.q: Which objective should guide a parent company’s decisions about interacting divisions?
options: Total company profit, including effects across divisions
The largest division’s reported profit alone
Equal reported profit in every division
The highest possible internal transfer price
fields.feedback: The supplied assessment supports total-company profit as the parent’s objective; division scores can conflict with it.

fields.q: Helping another division lowers A’s profit by $12,000 and raises B’s by $38,000. A refuses because its bonus uses only its own profit. What is the company consequence?
options: A locally rational refusal forgoes a $26,000 company gain
The refusal creates $12,000 because only A’s loss counts
Helping creates $50,000 by adding both absolute effects
Helping creates no value because internal effects cancel
fields.feedback: Both real divisional effects count: −12+38=26 thousand. The internal location of the gain does not make it disappear.

fields.q: A can help B at a real $16,000 cost; B gains $41,000. A’s manager refuses uncompensated help. An internal reimbursement of $22,000 would be accepted by both. What follows?
options: The reimbursement shares the $25,000 company gain; it does not create an extra company cost
The company gains $47,000 because reimbursement adds revenue
The company gains $3,000 because reimbursement is another resource cost
The project remains unprofitable because A originally wanted to refuse
fields.feedback: A gains 6,000 and B gains 19,000 after reimbursement. Their sum is the underlying 41,000−16,000=25,000 gain.

fields.q: What is a transfer price?
options: An accounting price charged on a sale between units of the same company
The unavoidable economic cost of every internal unit regardless of alternatives
The price paid by an independent external customer
A department’s budget unrelated to an internal sale
fields.feedback: The internal charge affects reported division profits and incentives; it is distinct from real opportunity cost.

fields.q: Internal supply has complete opportunity cost $32 and gives a buying division net value $50. At an internal charge of $58, what distortion can occur?
options: The buyer rejects a transfer worth $18 to the company
The company loses $8 because the internal charge exceeds buyer value
The company gains $26 because the seller’s accounting margin is $26
The buyer accepts because it observes the company gain
fields.feedback: Company value is 50−32=18, but the buyer sees 50−58=−8. The internal charge can block a valuable trade.

fields.q: A supplier has idle capacity, variable cost $26 per unit and no displaced outside sale. An internal 100-unit order requires an avoidable $500 setup. The buyer can purchase outside for $34 per unit. Which policy can support efficient trade?
options: Internal supply saves $300; a per-unit charge above $31 and below $34 can make both divisions better off
Charge exactly $26 and ignore setup because it is fixed for the order
Buy outside because setup makes every internal order inefficient
Any internal price creates the same incentives because it cancels for the company
fields.feedback: Internal cost is 2,600+500=3,100 versus 3,400 outside. An order price between complete cost and the buyer’s alternative shares the gain; marginal cost alone omits avoidable setup.

fields.q: A unit controls product prices and production costs and is judged on profit. What accountability form is this?
options: Profit center
Cost center evaluated on specified output cost
Revenue center judged only on sales
Shared-service unit with no outcome accountability
fields.feedback: Profit-center responsibility combines revenues and costs under meaningful managerial control.

fields.q: A support manager meets a cost target by cutting checks: $14,000 saved but $39,000 downstream defect costs. The manager cannot set selling prices. Which redesign fits?
options: Use controllable-cost and verified-service measures that recognize the $25,000 company loss
Reward the $14,000 saving because the unit is a cost center
Assign sales-price profit targets even though headquarters sets those prices
Remove service checks from evaluation so the target is easier to measure
fields.feedback: A cost center should deliver service efficiently, not minimize expenses without regard to value. Include attributable downstream harm while respecting controllability.

fields.q: One unit controls selling prices and costs; another supplies specified internal service and controls its delivery costs. Which evaluation pairing fits?
options: Profit accountability for the first; cost and service-quality accountability for the second
Cost-only accountability for both because every unit spends money
Revenue-only accountability for both because service supports sales
Profit accountability for the service unit using prices it cannot control
fields.feedback: Accountability should reflect decision rights. A cost center must still provide the specified service quality.

fields.q: Grouping engineers together and purchasing specialists together chiefly supports which advantage?
options: Shared expertise and specialization within functions
Independent responsibility for each complete product business
Automatic coordination between separate departments
Automatic agreement between personal and company objectives
fields.feedback: Functional grouping concentrates similar work and expertise; coordination and incentives still need attention.

fields.q: Marketing promises custom delivery before checking operations’ capacity and finance’s costs. Which process change most directly addresses the failure?
options: Review feasibility and contribution jointly before customer commitments
Raise marketing’s order-count target without changing approval
Judge operations only on unit cost after the promises are made
Require finance to approve spending without receiving delivery requirements
fields.feedback: Joint pre-commitment review brings relevant demand, capacity and cost information into the decision.

fields.q: Why can specialized departments need coordination?
options: One department’s decisions can change other departments’ costs and outcomes
Specialization prevents any department from knowing its own task
Separate reporting lines remove all shared dependencies
Coordination is needed only when the departments sell externally
fields.feedback: Specialized outputs often combine in a joint product or service, so local choices can impose cross-function effects.

fields.q: A firm has product businesses, each with its own marketing, operations and finance staff and responsibility for results. Which structure is this?
options: Multidivisional
Company-wide functional departments
One centralized shared-service cost center
Temporary cross-functional teams without business-line responsibility
fields.feedback: M-form groups responsibility around products, regions or businesses rather than only specialist functions.

fields.q: Why can product divisions help a diversified firm while still requiring headquarters coordination?
options: They clarify business results, but shared brands and investments create cross-division effects
They clarify results and therefore place every shared cost in the correct division automatically
They make product accountability unnecessary because headquarters owns the firm
They remove the need to compare duplicated specialist resources
fields.feedback: Business accountability improves visibility but does not internalize every spillover or eliminate duplication.

fields.q: Product divisions add $190,000 in accountability benefits but cost $115,000 in duplicated support and $40,000 in oversight. Functional teams add $100,000 at a $50,000 cost. Other effects equal, which design is supported?
options: Functional teams: $50,000 net versus $35,000 for divisions
Product divisions: $190,000 benefit exceeds $100,000
Product divisions: $75,000 net because oversight has no resource cost
Functional teams: $100,000 net because their expense is internal
fields.feedback: Compare all incremental effects: 190−115−40=35 and 100−50=50 thousand. M-form is a conditional design choice, not universally superior.

fields.q: A manager knowingly overstates expected expenses to negotiate an easier rewarded target. What is this?
options: Budget slack created through strategic reporting
An honest error caused by a later demand shock
A real productivity improvement with an unchanged target
An internal price that reallocates earned divisional profit
fields.feedback: The deliberate misreport and easier target distinguish gaming from forecast uncertainty.

fields.q: Unused funds automatically reduce next year’s budget, so a department buys unnecessary supplies in December. Which change targets the incentive?
options: Permit justified carryover while reviewing future resource needs
Require all funds to be spent earlier in the year
Reward expenditure totals regardless of service outcomes
Treat every unused dollar as proof of poor management
fields.feedback: Carryover can reduce spend-now pressure; reviewing needs limits slack rather than assuming all requests are truthful.

fields.q: Signup bonuses encourage risky customer approvals; annual profit targets encourage deferred maintenance; internal prices block profitable division trades. Which approach fits?
options: Match customer-quality, long-horizon and transfer controls to the respective omitted consequences
Apply a harder hiring test alone to all three current incentive problems
Raise all three existing bonuses without changing measured outcomes
Centralize decisions but preserve the same information gaps and reward measures
fields.feedback: The shared agency framework does not imply one identical remedy. Each omitted consequence requires a fitting control and evaluation of its costs.

fields.q: A hospital board values patient outcomes per resource used. Its chief officer controls staffing but earns a bonus for department size. Which change targets the conflict?
options: Make the officer principal because staffing authority was delegated
Raise the size bonus while holding outcome review fixed
Evaluate outcomes and controllable resource use rather than size alone
Judge only patient volume regardless of resource use or quality
fields.feedback: The officer is the board’s agent. A size metric rewards expansion without requiring valuable outcomes.

fields.q: Investors bear portfolio losses, while a manager gets large annual upside bonuses with little exposure to later losses. Risk is hidden. Which redesign best targets the conflict without treating all low returns as shirking?
options: Raise the same annual upside bonus to strengthen the current incentive
Combine longer-horizon risk-sensitive rewards with independent risk review
Punish every low annual return equally regardless of market conditions
Screen credentials once and treat later portfolio choices as known
fields.feedback: Payoff asymmetry encourages hidden risk. Longer-horizon rewards and verification address it while recognizing market noise.

fields.q: A lender funds an entrepreneur without learning a privately known high project risk. After funding, the entrepreneur secretly switches to an even riskier project. Which diagnosis fits?
options: Hidden type affects selection; hidden action affects the later project
Hidden action affects selection; hidden type is created only by switching
Both are moral hazard because the lender can lose money
Both are signaling because the entrepreneur chooses projects
fields.feedback: Risk relevant at selection differs from a later project choice. Loss itself is not the classification rule.

fields.q: A regional manager privately forecasts demand and later chooses unobserved selling effort. Headquarters uses the forecast to allocate staff and rewards sales above that same forecast. What combined redesign addresses both margins?
options: Reward bigger forecast errors because beating a low target proves strong effort
Audit only final sales and assume they reveal both original demand and effort
Verify planning evidence and reduce rewards for low forecasts, while using effort-relevant performance measures
Require a lower forecast but leave sales rewards and resource allocation unchanged
fields.feedback: The forecast can be strategically understated, and output also mixes effort with demand. Planning truthfulness and later effort need distinct controls.

fields.q: Agents paid for closed tickets mark unresolved cases complete. A closure-speed bonus also discourages difficult but valuable cases. Which design best addresses both distortions?
options: Measure reopen rates alone without checking avoided difficult cases
Pay more per closure while keeping the same self-reported status
Reward only easy cases because their outcomes are simpler to measure
Verify durable resolution and account for case difficulty, with selective audits
fields.feedback: Resolution verification limits false closure; difficulty-sensitive evaluation reduces avoidance of valuable hard cases. One measure alone leaves a gaming margin.

fields.q: A focused firm can share scarce specialists across products, but product-specific teams would duplicate those specialists. What supports retaining functional groups?
options: A rule that functions always outperform product divisions
The value of shared expertise and avoided duplication, subject to coordination costs
A claim that separate reporting lines make launches self-coordinating
A claim that specialists need no performance accountability
fields.feedback: Shared expertise can favor functions in this setting. The choice remains conditional on coordination and other costs.

fields.q: Functional teams preserve $80,000 in specialist-sharing benefits but require $25,000 in launch coordination. Product divisions avoid that coordination cost but sacrifice the sharing benefit and add $15,000 duplicate support. Other effects equal, which choice is supported?
options: Be indifferent because internal organization costs are only transfers
Choose divisions: avoiding $25,000 coordination settles the choice

fields.q: Next year’s sales target rises mechanically with this year’s sales. Managers delay profitable December orders into January to lower the benchmark. What redesign best addresses the problem without calling every forecast error misconduct?

fields.q: An insurer verifies applicants’ risk before enrollment and charges premiums reflecting that risk. This chiefly reduces...
