The insurer can pool independent workshop risks. Which contract can create gains for both parties?
options: Verified precautions and a premium strictly between $780 and $900; pooling does not itself restore care
Uncontrolled coverage at $800; compare the premium only with the original $600 expected claim
Verified precautions at $950; a positive insurer margin establishes a gain for the workshop too
Uncontrolled coverage below $900; adding more workshops removes the incentive effect of full coverage
fields.feedback: With verification, insurer cost is600+100+80=780 and the workshop’s maximum payment is900, leaving a mutually beneficial premium interval. Uncontrolled cost is850+100=950, above willingness to pay. Pooling independent losses reduces aggregate risk; it does not remove the behavior-induced increase in expected claims.

options: Screening to separate safer drivers from riskier drivers
Signaling initiated independently by the driver rather than the insurer
Monitoring used only to punish current carelessness, with no type inference
Risk pooling that changes the correlation of physical accident losses

fields.q: A policy’s safety-service feature appeals especially to firms that already had low loss rates. Lower-risk firms enroll disproportionately, but all enrollees reduce precautions after becoming insured. Average losses remain unchanged. What follows?
options: Favorable selection and worsening moral hazard may offset in the average
Unchanged average losses show neither selection nor care changed
Lower-risk entry shows adverse selection; reduced care is signaling
Better selection proves post-enrollment care incentives are adequate
fields.feedback: Lower-risk firms are more likely to participate: favorable selection. Reduced precautions after coverage are moral hazard. Aggregate losses can conceal opposite changes.

fields.q: An optional warranty raises a seller’s price by $24. Its expected total cost is $9 for reliable goods and $31 for unreliable goods. If each type maximizes its payoff, which outcome follows?
options: Reliable sellers offer; unreliable sellers do not
Both types offer because both receive the $24 premium
Neither type offers because warranty claims are possible
Unreliable sellers offer because their claims cost is higher
fields.feedback: Reliable sellers gain 24 − 9 = 15; unreliable sellers lose 24 − 31 = −7. Both comparisons support a separating signal.

fields.q: An insurer offers full coverage and a cheaper high-deductible plan. Low-risk customers prefer the cheaper plan; high-risk customers prefer full coverage because of expected claims. Care is held fixed. What makes this screening?
options: The insurer designed choices that reveal private risk through selection
Customers designed an independent credential to reveal their quality
The insurer directly observed every precaution after enrollment
The deductible changed care, its only possible economic effect
fields.feedback: The less-informed insurer created the menu and types choose differently. Holding care fixed isolates screening; a deductible can also affect behavior in another setting.

fields.q: A supplier voluntarily publishes an independently verified reliability certificate. A buyer separately requires a custom stress test before awarding a contract. Both reveal quality. How should they be classified?
options: The certificate is signaling; the buyer’s test is screening
Both are signaling because the supplier participates in both
Both are screening because third parties verify the results
The certificate is screening; the buyer’s test is signaling
fields.feedback: Classify by who initiates the mechanism. Independent verification makes evidence credible but does not determine whether it is screening or signaling.

fields.q: A platform displays verified seller histories and withholds payment until verified delivery. New buyers choose more reliable sellers, and existing sellers ship more promptly. Which evidence identifies each mechanism?
options: Changed seller choice shows selection; improved existing-seller effort shows an action response
Both changes show adverse selection because every seller has a history
Both changes show moral hazard because the platform holds money
Prompt shipment proves histories perfectly revealed every seller’s type
fields.feedback: Seller composition and behavior by a fixed set of sellers are different margins. Reputation informs selection; conditional payment can strengthen delivery incentives.

fields.q: History verification prevents $46,000 in expected buyer losses and costs $17,000. A marketplace deposit rule prevents $52,000, costs $8,000 to administer, and excludes reliable newcomers worth $35,000 in surplus. Other effects are equal. Which creates more net value?
options: Verified history: $29,000 versus $9,000 for deposits
Deposits: $44,000 versus $29,000 for verified history
Deposits: $52,000 versus $46,000 because prevention is the goal
Verified history: $46,000 because verification is an internal transfer
fields.feedback: History nets 46−17=29 thousand. Deposits net 52−8−35=9 thousand. Entry exclusion is a real cost.

fields.q: A platform bans sellers after one complaint, although complaints sometimes reflect delivery delays outside the seller’s control. Reliable new sellers begin leaving. Which revision best addresses this evidence?
options: Verify patterns and responsibility while retaining sanctions for proven misconduct
Ban after any unverified report to maximize the number removed
Remove all complaint records because some complaints are noisy
Treat remaining sellers as reliable once the first bans occur
fields.feedback: Noisy complaints can cause false exclusions and worsen selection. Verified patterns target poor quality or misconduct without abandoning discipline.

fields.q: A plan attracts applicants with high pre-existing risk and later sees insured customers reduce care. A manager proposes only an entry medical exam. Which evaluation is strongest?
options: The exam can improve selection, but care still needs incentives or monitoring
The exam addresses reduced care but reveals no pre-existing risk
A more accurate exam necessarily restores precautions after coverage
A deductible cannot affect care because it is written before coverage
fields.feedback: Entry screening informs type selection. It does not itself change the payoff from taking care. The date a contract is written does not determine the mechanism.

fields.q: A contractor can secretly skip a quality check costing $40 in effort. Skipping raises expected client repair costs by $150. Verification costs the client $25 per job and detects every skipped check, triggering a $70 loss of contractor pay. Which conclusion follows?
options: Verification deters skipping; the $65 checking-plus-verification cost is below $150 damage avoided
The contractor checks without control because the client’s loss exceeds $40
A $70 pay loss cannot deter skipping because it is below the client’s $150 loss
Verification destroys value because every control expense is a pure loss
fields.feedback: The contractor would save $40 by skipping but lose $70 when verified. Deterrence restores $40 of checking effort and costs $25 to verify, avoiding $150 expected damage: net gain $85.

fields.q: Workers can falsely mark undelivered parcels as complete. A firm monitors those marks, and raising completion bonuses increases false reporting. Which control most directly repairs the incentive?
options: Reward independently verified delivery and audit suspicious patterns
Raise the same completion bonus without verifying delivery
Screen driving ability at hiring but keep current payment rules
Pay for scanner activity because it is easier to observe
fields.feedback: Self-reported marks can be manipulated. Independent verification links rewards to delivery; ability screening does not correct the current reporting incentive.

fields.q: Four workers share a team bonus equally. One can spend effort worth $18 to raise the expected team bonus by $60. Colleagues’ effort is fixed and this worker’s effort is hidden. What follows?
options: The worker receives $15 of the gain and may withhold the effort
The worker receives $60 and therefore necessarily supplies effort
The worker receives $45 because the other three members each get $15
Hidden effort is irrelevant because total bonus gain exceeds effort cost
fields.feedback: The private return is 60/4=15, below 18. Equal sharing dilutes the individual incentive even though the total bonus gain exceeds the effort cost.

fields.q: After a loan, a borrower secretly chooses a project. The safe project returns $120 for sure; the risky project returns $220 with probability 0.5 and zero otherwise. Debt repayment is $100 when feasible and the borrower has limited liability. Ignoring other costs, what conflict arises?
options: The borrower prefers risky residual $60 over $20, although total expected return falls from $120 to $110
The borrower prefers safe payoff $120 over $110 because debt is irrelevant
The lender prefers risky repayment $110 over safe repayment $100
Both parties prefer risk because its successful return is $220
fields.feedback: Borrower residuals are 120−100=20 and 0.5×(220−100)=60. Total expected risky return is 110, below 120; expected lender repayment falls from 100 to 50.

fields.q: Owners want net company value; a manager earns a revenue bonus. The manager privately knows a campaign adds $80,000 revenue but $95,000 incremental costs. Which change addresses the conflict while preserving local knowledge?
options: Reward verified incremental contribution and retain local campaign discretion
Raise the revenue bonus so the manager values growth more strongly
Retest ability without changing the manager’s campaign rewards
Require central approval without obtaining the manager’s cost information
fields.feedback: The campaign loses $15,000 despite higher revenue. Contribution pay includes omitted costs while preserving informed local choices; credible verification still matters.

fields.q: A manager hired after an ability test performs well on isolated tasks but neglects teamwork after individual-output bonuses begin. Output also falls during a power outage. Which diagnosis fits?
options: Separate bonus-induced teamwork distortion from the outage; neither proves the ability test failed
Treat both teamwork neglect and the outage as low pre-hire ability
Treat the outage as shirking and the bonus response as adverse selection
Retest ability only because successful screening removes later conflict
fields.feedback: Ability, effort allocation and uncontrollable shocks are different. Bonus-related neglect points to incentives; the outage does not establish low effort.

fields.q: Account-opening bonuses cause agents to approve customers they privately expect to default. Repayment-only pay would also penalize agents for economy-wide shocks. Which redesign fits both concerns?
options: Reward verified customer quality and repayment adjusted for common shocks
Pay more per account while ignoring customer default information
Use raw repayment and treat every macroeconomic shock as agent effort
Remove quality checks because customer outcomes are uncertain
fields.feedback: Rewards should account for customer quality without treating all default variation as controllable. Verification and shock adjustment address distinct problems.

fields.q: A firm loses $70,000 annually from hidden managerial actions. Broad control prevents $55,000 but costs $38,000 plus $12,000 in delays. Targeted control prevents $42,000 and costs $20,000 without delays. Which gives greater net improvement?
options: Targeted control: $22,000 versus $5,000 for broad control
Broad control: $55,000 versus $42,000 because prevention is larger
Broad control: $17,000 versus $22,000, so its coverage wins
Targeted control: $50,000 because all remaining loss disappears
fields.feedback: Broad control gains 55−38−12=5 thousand; targeted gains 42−20=22 thousand. Remaining loss is not zero, but eliminating more loss need not be optimal.

fields.q: Branches know urgent customer needs; headquarters knows shared-capacity constraints. Local volume bonuses cause overpromising, but central approval loses time-sensitive orders. Which design uses both kinds of information?
options: Delegate routine promises with current capacity costs and margin rewards; escalate major spillovers
Delegate every promise and keep local volume rewards unchanged
Centralize every promise without collecting current local demand
Keep local authority but report only historical revenue, excluding capacity costs
fields.feedback: Current resource information and aligned rewards preserve speed while internalizing spillovers. Large cross-unit effects can still require central coordination.

fields.q: A purchasing manager accepts supplier gifts and chooses higher-cost inputs. Owners cannot observe gifts but can verify comparable bids and product quality. Which control fits the diagnosis?
options: Require documented bid comparisons and reward verified purchasing value
Retest technical knowledge without changing purchase review
Reward supplier-meeting counts regardless of purchase outcomes
Raise the fixed purchasing budget to reduce the need for comparisons
fields.feedback: Private gifts conflict with the owner’s purchasing objective. Verifiable comparisons and value-related accountability target the distorted choice.

fields.q: A parent company can close Division A and save $70,000 of avoidable cost. A currently earns $40,000 revenue, while its support enables B to earn $50,000 contribution that would disappear if A closed. A also reports $30,000 of allocated headquarters cost that would remain. What should headquarters do?
options: Keep A: closing lowers company profit by $20,000 despite A’s reported loss
Close A: its $60,000 reported loss is the company gain from closure
Close A: $70,000 avoidable cost exceeds A’s $40,000 revenue
Keep A: all allocated headquarters cost disappears only if both divisions close
fields.feedback: Closing saves70 but loses40+50, reducing company profit by20 thousand. The unchanged30 allocation is not an incremental saving. A’s reported loss omits its support for B and includes an unavoidable allocation.

fields.q: Division A can help B at a real cost of $18,000. B gains $44,000 before internal charges, but the project also harms another company unit by $6,000. Headquarters charges that harm to B. A and B can both veto the project and each requires a strictly positive gain. For an internal payment P from B to A, which policy creates company value and lets both approve?
options: Choose $18,000 < P < $38,000; company gain is $20,000 regardless of P
Choose $18,000 < P < $44,000; the charge for harm does not affect B’s veto
Choose P above $38,000; protecting A’s reported profit is sufficient for approval
Choose P = $18,000; company value alone ensures A has a strictly positive gain
fields.feedback: A gains P−18 thousand; B gains 44−6−P=38−P. Both gains are strictly positive only between 18 and 38. Company value is 44−18−6=20 thousand: internal payment and the charge cancel in consolidation, while the real harm remains. Local consent and total value are separate conditions.

fields.q: A supplier division is at capacity. It sells components outside for $68, paying $4 in selling expenses avoided on internal orders. Production costs $37 either way. A sister division can buy the same component outside for $61. What should the company do?
options: Buy outside: internal supply forgoes $64 net external revenue to avoid a $61 purchase
Transfer internally: $37 production cost is below the $61 outside price
Transfer internally: any price below $68 creates company value
Be indifferent: internal prices cancel, so sourcing has no real effect
fields.feedback: At capacity the internal opportunity cost is 68−4=$64. Outside purchase at $61 is $3 cheaper; production cost alone misses displaced sales.

fields.q: A product manager controls prices and production costs but shifts support costs to a shared unit. Reported product profit rises $50,000 while uncharged support costs rise $75,000. Which evaluation change fits?
options: Keep profit accountability but include attributable support costs and service effects
Reclassify the unit as a cost center and ignore its pricing decisions
Keep the current measure because costs outside the unit are irrelevant
Reward revenue alone so allocation disputes no longer affect bonuses
fields.feedback: The unit has profit-center rights. Its measure needs the costs it causes; otherwise reported gain conceals a $25,000 company loss.

fields.q: A support unit controls effort and cost but not sales prices. Cutting checks saves $12,000 and causes $30,000 in downstream defects; preserving checks avoids both. Which accountability rule fits?
options: Evaluate controllable costs with verified quality and downstream defect effects
Reward the lowest support cost without a service condition
Evaluate sales prices set only by headquarters
Remove accountability because some outcomes are outside the unit
fields.feedback: A cost center should deliver specified service efficiently. Quality and attributable downstream effects discourage a saving that loses $18,000 overall.

fields.q: Two products share scarce engineers. Functional engineering saves $120,000 through shared expertise but launch delays cost $90,000. Separate product divisions would remove those delays but lose the shared savings and add $40,000 in duplicated support. Joint launch authority within the functional structure costs $25,000 and reduces delay losses to $30,000. Which redesign and governance choice best follow?
options: Keep shared engineering with joint launch authority; its $65,000 net saving requires authority across functions
Create product divisions; removing $90,000 of delay outweighs all specialization effects
Keep current functional targets; the full $120,000 saving is the relevant net gain
Create joint launch meetings without shared authority; assume the same delay reduction at no governance cost
fields.feedback: Relative to neither sharing nor its delays, the current functional net is 120−90=30 thousand; joint authority nets 120−25−30=65. Divisionalization loses sharing and adds40 in support cost. The stated benefit depends on cross-functional authority; meetings alone do not resolve conflicting departmental decisions.

fields.q: A firm groups engineers by technical specialty to share expertise. Headquarters approves every routine technical change, causing delays; product teams would duplicate scarce experts. What change targets the delay while preserving the stated specialization benefit?
options: Delegate routine technical decisions within the functional units, with escalation for cross-product effects
Create product divisions because functional grouping necessarily requires all decisions at headquarters
Keep every approval centralized because shared expertise eliminates the cost of delay
Let each specialist make every cross-product commitment without coordination
fields.feedback: Functional grouping describes who works together, not a requirement that headquarters decide everything. Delegating routine decisions can use specialist information without duplicating teams; escalation remains useful when a decision affects several products.

fields.q: Marketing can promise a delivery date only operations knows is feasible. Operations can save overtime by postponing it, but only marketing knows the customer penalty. Both report their own costs accurately; neither sees the other’s information. Which first redesign targets the problem?
options: Share capacity and customer-penalty information before joint commitments, then evaluate the combined result
Increase audits of each cost report; truthful local reports already provide all needed coordination
Give marketing unilateral date authority because it knows customers better
Give operations unilateral date authority because overtime is the only relevant real cost
fields.feedback: The failure is fragmented information and decision rights, not demonstrated false reporting. Joint commitments need both capacity and customer consequences. Combined evaluation also avoids rewarding one function for imposing losses on the other.

fields.q: Sales proposes a rush order with $42,000 contribution before rush costs. Operations would spend $9,000 and displace $38,000 of other contribution. Overtime costing $11,000 in addition to the rush costs could avoid displacement. Sales is rewarded only for its own contribution; operations is rewarded only for cutting expense. Which coordinated decision and measure are supported?
options: Use overtime: $22,000 net gain; reward both functions on the combined incremental result
Reject: the ordinary schedule loses $5,000, so the overtime alternative need not be evaluated
Use overtime: sales should keep its contribution metric and operations absorb the cost penalty
Accept without overtime: the displaced order is not a new invoice and can be omitted
fields.feedback: The ordinary schedule nets 42−9−38=−5 thousand. Overtime nets 42−9−11=22. Sales alone omits production effects; cost-only operations can reject worthwhile overtime. Sharing the full incremental result aligns the functions while retaining local capacity information.

fields.q: Product divisions would improve accountability by $160,000 annually but duplicate support at $105,000 and add $35,000 coordination costs. Functional units with launch teams would gain $85,000 at a $50,000 cost. Other effects equal, which change is better?
options: Functional units with teams: $35,000 net versus $20,000 for divisions
Product divisions: $160,000 exceeds the teams’ $85,000 benefit
Product divisions: $55,000 net because coordination is not a cost
Functional units with teams: $85,000 net because team costs are internal
fields.feedback: Divisions net 160−105−35=20 thousand; teams net 85−50=35 thousand. Actual effects, not structure labels, determine the ranking.

fields.q: Managers submit forecasts and earn bonuses for beating targets derived from them. One deliberately understates known demand; another honestly forecasts but misses after an unexpected shock. Which diagnosis and redesign fit?
options: The first creates slack; the second is not shown to game. Separate forecasts from negotiable bonus hurdles
Both game because every forecast error shows dishonest reporting
Only the second games because a missed target proves low effort
Neither can game because the submitted numbers concern the future
fields.feedback: Intentional misrepresentation for an easier reward threshold is gaming. Uncertainty can cause honest errors; forecast use and rewards should distinguish them.

fields.q: Departments inflate next year’s requests because headquarters routinely cuts every request by 10%. They also buy unwanted equipment because unused funds reduce future allocations. Allowing carryover would remove the spending deadline but leave managers’ private estimates of need. Which redesign addresses both behaviors without assuming information becomes free?
options: Allow justified carryover and review requests against activity evidence; weigh verification cost and remaining slack
Allow unlimited carryover and retain uniform cuts; ending the deadline also makes requests truthful
Ban carryover and stop uniform cuts; truthful requests would eliminate waste from expiring funds
Keep both rules and reward low year-end balances; tighter measurement aligns spending with real need
fields.feedback: Carryover reduces the incentive to exhaust allocations. Replacing predictable uniform cuts with evidence-based review weakens request inflation. Managers still know more about needs, and verification consumes resources; neither truthful budgets nor zero slack is guaranteed.

fields.q: A repair firm finds both weak initial technical skill and rushed work under pay per completed job. A work sample identifies technical skill before hiring. Paying for verified durable repairs instead of job counts nets $13 per repair rather than $6, after callback and verification costs. Removing verification saves $4, but then technicians can hide callbacks. Which design follows from these facts?
options: Use the work sample and verified durable-repair pay; each addresses a different information problem
Use the work sample and job-count pay; selecting skilled workers removes the incentive to rush
Use durable-repair pay without verification; add $4 to the verified plan’s net value
Use verified durable-repair pay without the work sample; effort rewards establish initial technical skill
fields.feedback: The work sample screens ability before hiring; durable-repair pay changes effort incentives afterward. Its $13 net already includes verification. A $4 saving cannot be added while assuming callbacks remain truthfully reported. Skill and effort are distinct margins.

fields.q: A purchasing manager knows supplier quality better than headquarters but receives bonuses for the lowest invoice price. Defects rise after cheaper suppliers are selected; a plant outage also raises total cost. Centralizing all purchases would delay urgent orders. Which redesign follows from all three facts?
options: Retest purchasing knowledge alone, assuming verified expertise removes the incentive to choose cheap defective inputs
Keep local choice and invoice-price bonuses, but treat every increase in total cost as low purchasing effort
Centralize every purchase and retain invoice-price bonuses, treating approval delay as irrelevant
Keep bounded local choice, verify supplier quality, and reward cost including defects while separating outage costs
fields.feedback: The manager has useful local information and a reward conflict: invoice savings omit defects. Verified quality and defect-inclusive costs target that conflict. An outage outside the manager’s control should not be treated as effort. Bounded delegation avoids needless central delay while retaining review for large effects.

options: The pool changed; a care incentive alone does not establish improved selection
Unchanged rates within groups show that the enrollment mix cannot raise average claims
The rising average establishes less care by each insured customer
The deductible necessarily improves pool composition whenever it changes loss sharing

fields.q: A new insurance contract attracts safer applicants but reduces each enrollee’s precautions. Average claims stay unchanged. Management wants to keep the entry advantage and improve care. Which evaluation and redesign best fit?
options: Keep the contract unchanged because average claims show neither mechanism changed
Separate selection from behavior; compare care incentives and monitoring while checking effects on safer applicants’ participation
Tighten entry screening only because safer applicants cannot reduce care
Raise loss sharing without checking whether safer applicants leave or protection loses value
fields.feedback: Favorable composition and worsening care can offset. A care reform must be evaluated for its behavior effect, selection effect and lost insurance value rather than judged only by average claims.

options: Use a harder entry test as the sole remedy for both later problems
Increase output bonuses without adjusting for storms or teamwork
Screening helps selection; pay still needs to address noise and unmeasured cooperative effort
Use storm-affected output alone to decide which applicants had low ability

fields.q: Verified seller histories cost $18,000 and prevent $32,000 in buyer losses. A deposit rule costs $6,000, prevents $25,000, and excludes reliable newcomers worth $12,000 in surplus. Other effects are equal. Which choice and switching condition are correct?
options: Choose deposits; their $19,000 benefit after administration exceeds history’s $14,000
Choose history; deposits become better only if excluded surplus falls below $5,000
Choose history; deposits become better whenever excluded surplus is below $12,000
Choose deposits; excluding sellers is an accounting transfer rather than a real cost
fields.feedback: History nets 14,000. Deposits net 19,000−12,000=7,000. Deposits beat history only if exclusion cost is below 19,000−14,000=5,000.

fields.q: Full coverage causes expected avoidable loss of 40. A deductible prevents 18 but sacrifices 13 in valued risk protection. Inspections prevent 15 and cost 7. Using both prevents 24, with both costs still incurred. Other effects are equal. Which design has greatest net value?
options: Both: net 17, because only inspection expense counts
Both: net 13, because separate prevention benefits can be added
Deductible alone: net 18, because lost risk protection is not a resource cost
Inspections alone: net 8, versus 5 for deductible and 4 for both
fields.feedback: Inspections net 15−7=8; deductible nets 18−13=5; both net 24−13−7=4. Prevention overlaps and lost risk protection is a real welfare cost.

options: Lower entrant default establishes that covenants stopped project switching
Selection may have improved; the continuing project switches show a post-loan control gap
Later project switches identify only a pre-loan ability problem
Good credit screening makes enforcement of project limits unnecessary

fields.q: Warehouse staff receive per-scan bonuses. Duplicate scans raise recorded output, rushed packing raises damage, and workers stop helping teammates. Paying for unique shipments removes duplicates but leaves damage and teamwork unmeasured. Which redesign best targets all three distortions while recognizing control costs?
options: Use verified undamaged shipments and a team component; compare audit cost and free-riding with the gains
Use unique-shipment pay alone; eliminating duplicate counts also removes damage and teamwork incentives
Pay solely for team shipment counts; shared pay removes both damage incentives and free-riding
Pay for individual undamaged shipments alone; accurate individual output also rewards helping teammates
fields.feedback: Unique identifiers address duplicate counts; damage verification addresses quality; a team component can reward cooperation but creates a free-riding risk. The combined design must earn more than its audit and incentive costs. No single reported count establishes all three outcomes.

fields.q: Managers privately choose purchasing effort. Relative to no control, targeted audits prevent $25,000 in losses and cost $12,000 plus $3,000 in delay. Broad audits prevent $31,000 and cost $24,000 plus $10,000 in delay. With targeted audits, an additional verified-savings bonus would prevent another $8,000 in losses but cost $5,000 to pay and verify. Managers can inflate reported savings if verification is dropped. Which policy is best on these stated effects?
options: Targeted audits alone: $10,000 net benefit; added controls necessarily waste resources
Targeted audits plus the verified bonus: $13,000 net benefit; keep verification
Broad audits: $31,000 benefit; maximize prevented losses rather than net value
Targeted audits with an unverified bonus: count the same $8,000 saving at lower cost
fields.feedback: Targeted audits net 25−12−3=10 thousand; adding the verified bonus nets another 8−5=3. Broad audits net 31−24−10=−3. The saving estimate depends on verification, so dropping it does not preserve the incentive effect. Compare total control value, including administration, delay and gaming.

options: The local changes lose 10 overall; local knowledge alone does not justify unrestricted menu authority
The changes gain 45 because purchasing losses belong to another unit
The changes gain 20 because ingredient cost is an internal charge
The changes lose 85 because customer value should be omitted
Restore revenue-only rewards because delay alone establishes delegation is superior
Compare central approval with delegated margin-based pay and targeted audits, including both delay and control costs
Retain full central approval because improvement over the old design proves optimality
Delegate with margin pay but exclude audit cost and lost-order effects from comparison

fields.q: Division A can sell every unit outside for $74, with $41 production cost and $6 external selling expense. B can buy an equivalent verified unit outside for $72. Internal trade avoids A’s selling expense but requires a quality check charged to B. Two equally effective checks cost $5 or $1 per unit. With each division able to veto and requiring a strictly positive gain, which control and transfer-price policy creates company value?
options: Use the $5 check and $41 < P < $67; production cost alone is A’s opportunity cost
Use the $1 check and $68 < P < $72; B’s testing charge does not affect consent
Use the $5 check and $68 < P < $72; internal testing expense cancels in consolidation
Use the $1 check and $68 < P < $71; the company gains $3 per unit
fields.feedback: A’s opportunity cost is 74−6=68. With the $1 check, B can pay less than 72−1=71, leaving company gain 72−68−1=3. The $5 check leaves B’s ceiling 67 below A’s floor 68 and destroys $1 of company value. The accounting transfer cancels; actual quality-control resources and forgone external sales do not.

fields.q: Headquarters sets prices, product mix and demand forecasts for a service unit; its manager controls staffing and purchasing. Total-profit targets have caused service cuts when headquarters discounts prices. A proposal would give the unit customer and pricing decisions but those prices could divert sales from a sister unit. Which evaluation design fits both stages?
options: Now use total profit despite central prices; with pricing rights, use only controllable cost
Now use controllable cost with service standards; with pricing rights, use profit adjusted for effects on the sister unit
Now use cost alone despite service cuts; with pricing rights, use unadjusted local profit
Now use revenue alone; with pricing rights, charge every headquarters expense regardless of controllability
fields.feedback: A cost-center measure fits current rights only with service safeguards. Broader revenue and cost control can support profit-center accountability, but local profit omitting diverted sister-unit sales may conflict with company profit. Rights, measurement and cross-unit incentives must change together.

fields.q: Functional units with launch teams cost $90,000 and recover $150,000 of losses. Product divisions recover $230,000, add $140,000 duplicate support and $45,000 oversight. Other effects are equal. Which choice and condition for reversal are correct?
options: Choose divisions; oversight is an internal allocation with no real cost
Choose divisions; the $230,000 recovery exceeds the teams’ $150,000
Choose teams; divisions become better whenever duplication is below $140,000
Choose functional teams; divisions become better if duplicate support falls below $125,000
fields.feedback: Teams net 60,000; divisions net 45,000. Divisions beat teams when 230,000−45,000−duplication exceeds 60,000, or duplication is below 125,000.

fields.q: A firm compares two pre-hire tests and hires every passer. Test A admits 72 capable and 8 weak applicants and costs $1,000. Test B admits 64 capable and 2 weak applicants and costs $4,000. Each capable hire creates $200 net value; each weak hire loses $500, after pay and other hiring costs. Both groups can later shirk if effort incentives are poor. Which conclusion follows?
options: Choose A: $9,400 net versus $7,800; its higher weak share does not remove the need for effort incentives
Choose B: the lowest weak share necessarily yields the highest total net hiring value
Choose A: $9,400 net; selecting capable applicants also resolves later hidden effort
Choose B: compare $11,800 before test cost with A’s $9,400 after test cost
fields.feedback: A nets 72×200−8×500−1000=9400; B nets 64×200−2×500−4000=7800. B has a lower weak share (2/66 versus 8/80), but rejects more capable applicants and costs more. Pre-hire screening does not guarantee effort after hiring.

fields.q: An insurer expects 60 low-risk firms with annual claims of $24 each and 40 high-risk firms with claims of $96. Low-risk firms will pay at most $50; high-risk firms at most $120. A pooled $60 premium drives low-risk firms away. Alternatively, accurate risk verification costs $4 per insured firm and permits premiums of $40 and $108 for the respective types. Care is unchanged and there are no other costs. Which comparison is correct?
options: The verified plan earns $14.40 per policy after verification because the fee is an internal transfer
The pooled plan keeps its forecast $7.20 margin; verified pricing need not account for who enrolls
The verified plan loses $4 per policy because risk classification cannot create value without changing care
The pooled plan loses $36 per enrollee; verified pricing retains both types and earns $10.40 per policy on average
fields.feedback: The original mixed expected claim is 0.6×24+.4×96=52.8, but only high-risk firms accept $60, so the actual pooled margin is 60−96=−36. Both verified premiums meet willingness to pay. Margins after verification are 40−24−4=12 and 108−96−4=8; their weighted average is 0.6×12+.4×8=10.4. Selection and verification costs jointly determine viability; care does not change.

fields.q: What is transferred when a buyer purchases insurance?
options: Financial exposure to a specified loss
The physical event’s probability by payment alone
The buyer’s preferences about uncertainty
Every precaution decision to the insurer
fields.feedback: Insurance reallocates financial risk, not the event or the buyer’s risk preferences.

fields.q: Why can a risk-averse buyer pay more than expected claims?
options: Reduced uncertainty can be worth the premium loading
The loading increases expected cash wealth by itself
Risk aversion means expecting a claim with certainty
Paying a premium makes insured events independent
fields.feedback: Value includes risk protection, not only expected monetary payments.

fields.q: Which fact identifies adverse selection rather than private information alone?
options: Hidden type changes who trades toward less favorable participants
A party reduces care because a contract shifts losses
An informed party offers a credible quality commitment
An uninformed party observes and prices each type directly
fields.feedback: Adverse selection concerns participant composition. Hidden action is a different mechanism.

options: The evidence concerns selection of lower-risk types, not a post-contract change in action
Moral hazard is identified whenever average claims differ across groups
Lower losses establish that coverage caused safer behavior
Every insured-versus-uninsured difference is adverse selection
Screening starts with the less-informed employer seeking information
Screening is defined by who takes the test rather than who designs it
Every employer-required test is a voluntary applicant signal
A pre-hire test directly observes later workplace effort

fields.q: An insurer designs two policies that private risk types choose differently. Is this compatible with screening?
options: Yes; the insurer created the information-revealing menu
No; screening requires seeing every type directly
No; every customer choice is automatically signaling
Yes; every deductible only changes care after coverage
fields.feedback: Screening can induce information through choices. Who designed the mechanism matters.

fields.q: What must a proposed quality signal establish?
options: It is expensive even if both types benefit equally
High-quality types choose it while low-quality imitation is unattractive
Buyers see the claim even if every type copies it freely
The buyer designed the test, making the seller the initiator
fields.feedback: Credibility requires informative type-dependent choices, not expense or visibility alone.

fields.q: How can a completed purchase inform someone who has not bought yet?
options: Past performance informs the next buyer’s quality expectations
It observes the next buyer’s future product use
It transfers the next buyer’s loss to the past buyer
It makes the next transaction’s outcome certain
fields.feedback: Past data inform a new selection while remaining imperfect evidence.

fields.q: Why verify that a review came from a real purchase?
options: To improve the credibility of quality evidence
To guarantee the seller’s next action
To reveal every buyer’s willingness to pay
To remove the need to consider recent seller changes
fields.feedback: Authenticity limits manipulation without ensuring complete or current information.

fields.q: What distinguishes moral hazard from adverse selection?
options: Hidden action under incentives versus hidden type affecting selection
Any loss after a contract versus any profit before one
Unobservable information versus perfectly observable information
Any insurance contract versus any employment contract
fields.feedback: Identify the private variable and distorted decision; timing helps but is not the entire mechanism.

fields.q: How does monitoring differ from incentive pay?
options: Monitoring improves action information; pay changes rewards
Monitoring changes only entry selection; pay reveals every action
Both require observing every action perfectly
Pay affects behavior only when fixed rather than contingent
fields.feedback: Information and private rewards are different, potentially complementary control margins.

fields.q: Which evidence most clearly identifies shirking?
options: Required effort is deliberately reduced when unobservable
Output falls after equipment failure with unchanged effort
An applicant lacks a skill before hiring
A worker completes assigned tasks with less unnecessary motion
fields.feedback: Hidden reduced effort differs from bad luck, hidden ability and efficiency.

fields.q: Why can moral hazard remain after a lender accurately screens borrower type?
options: The borrower still chooses projects after funding
Screening makes every later choice observable
Borrower type and chosen project are the same fixed fact
Promised interest necessarily aligns risk preferences
fields.feedback: Selection information does not remove post-funding discretion or payoff conflict.

fields.q: What must an aligned incentive reward?
options: Choices advancing the principal’s actual objective
Any easy-to-count activity regardless of value
Reported outcomes without checking manipulation
A larger payment regardless of which actions earn it
fields.feedback: Stronger incentives cannot repair a measure rewarding the wrong outcome.

fields.q: Which costs belong in a comparison of agency controls?
options: Resources and other incremental harms caused by the control
Only invoices labeled monitoring, excluding delay
Only remaining misconduct, excluding control resources
Only agent bonuses, excluding productive-work effects
fields.feedback: Controls can use resources and delay or distort decisions. Count complete consequences.

options: The manager has delegated discretion even though oversight remains
Later central review means the manager never had authority
Collecting information alone gives the same decision rights
A refund limit means each permitted refund needs prior central approval

fields.q: Why is higher division profit insufficient to establish parent success?
options: The choice may impose larger real costs on other units
Every division gain is just an internal transfer
The parent should disregard division costs
Coordination makes total profit impossible to calculate
fields.feedback: Include real effects across units and cancel purely internal payments.

fields.q: Which responsibility distinguishes a profit center from a cost center?
options: Revenues and costs determining profit
Only the cost of specified service
Only sales regardless of costs
No accountability because headquarters owns the unit
fields.feedback: Profit responsibility includes revenue and costs; relevant decision control matters.

fields.q: What should cost-center efficiency mean?
options: Deliver specified service quality with appropriate cost control
Reduce expense regardless of service lost
Maximize revenue from prices set elsewhere
Spend every budgeted dollar
fields.feedback: A cost center has a service obligation; lower expense alone is not greater value.

fields.q: What makes an organization functional?
options: Grouping work by specialty such as engineering or finance
Giving each product business all its own functions
Centralizing every decision regardless of grouping
Evaluating every unit only on profit
fields.feedback: Specialty grouping differs from authority location and performance measures.

fields.q: When should a department include effects on another unit?
options: When its choice changes that unit’s real costs or outcomes
Only when the other unit pays it cash
Only when both units have identical targets
Never when units are separately accountable
fields.feedback: Real dependencies matter even without an internal invoice.

fields.q: What is central to a multidivisional structure?
options: Business-line or regional responsibility combining relevant functions
Company-wide grouping solely by technical specialty
Delegating every choice with no headquarters role
Evaluating every operating unit only on cost
fields.feedback: Divisions own broader business results; headquarters can manage shared strategy/resources.

fields.q: What distinguishes budget gaming from an honest forecast error?
options: Deliberate reporting or timing to obtain an easier rewarded target
Any forecast-versus-actual difference
Any resource request to headquarters
Any year with uncertain demand
fields.feedback: Identify strategic intent and the reward rule rather than inaccurate prediction alone.

fields.q: Why can automatic cuts to next year’s budget cause waste now?
options: Managers may spend unused funds to protect future allocations
Unused funds always prove lower future need
Every December purchase raises company value
The rule reveals resource needs without verification
fields.feedback: Future allocation tied to spending can reward unnecessary purchases. Useful spending is different.

fields.q: A shop values coverage at $180. Expected claims plus administration cost $120. At a $150 premium, what is true?
options: Both gain: shop surplus $30 and insurer expected profit $30
Only the insurer gains because expected claims are below the premium
Both gain $60 because willingness to pay exceeds insurer cost by $60
Neither gains unless the shop files a claim
fields.feedback: The buyer and insurer split the $60 potential surplus. Risk protection has value before the loss outcome.

fields.q: An insurer adds shops with independent local theft risks. Why can this improve risk bearing?
options: Losses need not occur together, making average claims more predictable
Every shop has the same realized loss in each year
Expected claims disappear as the number of shops rises
Independence follows from charging the same premium
fields.feedback: Pooling independent exposures reduces average-claim variability without eliminating expected loss or common shocks.

fields.q: At one pooled premium, owners of unreliable machines are more eager to buy breakdown coverage than owners of reliable machines. Care does not change afterward. Which evidence matters?
options: Types choosing coverage have higher pre-existing expected costs
All owners reduce maintenance because coverage pays losses
The insurer observes and prices every machine’s condition
The same machines became less reliable because premiums were paid
fields.feedback: Higher-cost types disproportionately enroll. Unchanged care isolates selection.

fields.q: A buyer requires suppliers to submit independently tested samples before awarding a contract. What is this?
options: Buyer-initiated screening of private quality
Supplier-initiated signaling independent of the requirement
Monitoring effort on the completed contract
Insurance against the buyer’s future sales risk
fields.feedback: The buyer initiated a pre-selection test. Verification supports credibility without changing the initiator.

fields.q: An insurer offers cheaper high-deductible coverage and more expensive full coverage. With care fixed, lower-risk customers choose the former. What is revealed?
options: Plan choices help distinguish risk types
Choices directly reveal each later precaution
The menu insures the firm against shirking
Low deductibles prove improved customer care
fields.feedback: Type-dependent contract choice can screen risk; care is held fixed.

fields.q: A voluntary guarantee earns $16 extra revenue. Expected claims cost reliable sellers $5 and unreliable sellers $23. Which pattern supports signaling?
options: Reliable sellers offer; unreliable sellers decline
Both offer because extra revenue is positive
Unreliable sellers offer because claims are larger
Neither offers because claims are possible
fields.feedback: Net gains are 11 and −7. Low-quality imitation is unattractive.

fields.q: High seller ratings are mostly old; recent verified disputes are rising. Which response fits?
options: Weigh authenticity and recent evidence alongside the lifetime average
Ignore all reviews because past evidence cannot inform current quality
Treat lifetime review count as proof recent disputes are irrelevant
Infer every recent dispute arose from buyer moral hazard
fields.feedback: Freshness and verification matter. Neither blind trust nor discarding all evidence follows.

fields.q: A platform has verified repeat misrepresentation but noisy one-off complaints. Which sanction policy better supports quality?
options: Investigate verified patterns before exclusion
Ban after every unverified complaint
Keep sellers despite proven misrepresentation
Treat every surviving seller as certainly reliable
fields.feedback: Evidence-based exclusion limits unreliable participation and false removal of good sellers.

fields.q: After full travel reimbursement begins, employees privately choose unnecessary premium services. Which control targets the problem?
options: Verify business need or make employees bear extra discretionary cost
Retest credentials without changing reimbursement rules
Assume travelers were high-risk types before employment
Raise reimbursement limits without reviewing choices
fields.feedback: Hidden spending responds to shifted costs. Verification or exposure targets behavior.

fields.q: Workers are paid per self-reported inspection. Some reports are false. Which monitoring change targets the gap?
options: Independently verify a sample of actual inspections
Count the same reports more frequently without verification
Check applicant credentials but not current inspections
Increase payment for each unchecked report
fields.feedback: Observing a manipulable report is not verifying the underlying action.

fields.q: Three workers share a bonus equally. One can spend effort worth $12 to raise the total bonus by $24. Their effort is hidden. Why might they not contribute?
options: Their own reward rises only $8, below effort cost
Their own reward rises $24, above effort cost
The team receives only $8 in total
Sharing the bonus reveals each worker’s effort
fields.feedback: The worker captures one-third of the gain; equal sharing dilutes the private incentive.

fields.q: A screened borrower secretly switches to a project with more private upside and more lender loss. Which remedy targets this?
options: Enforce project covenants and monitoring with meaningful borrower downside
Repeat the original credit check but leave later actions unrestricted
Raise repayment and assume risk incentives improve automatically
Publish customer reviews unrelated to the project
fields.feedback: Project controls and downside exposure address post-loan action; entry screening alone cannot.

options: The supplier offer proves low ability before hiring
The manager becomes principal because they choose suppliers
Formal delegation makes private benefits irrelevant
Private benefits can distort a decision made on the owner’s behalf

fields.q: Revenue bonuses lead staff to discount enough to raise revenue but lower contribution. Which change targets the gap?
options: Reward verified contribution after relevant costs
Increase the same revenue bonus
Reward invoice counts instead of revenue
Screen staff again without changing rewards
fields.feedback: Profit includes costs. Change what is rewarded, not only bonus size.

fields.q: An audit prevents $20,000 of misconduct but costs $9,000 and delays decisions worth $4,000. What is its net benefit?
fields.feedback: 20,000−9,000−4,000=7,000. Prevention is a benefit; resources and delay are costs.

fields.q: Branches discount to capture sister branches’ customers under volume bonuses. Central coordination may respond slowly. What should headquarters compare?
options: Coordination gains against delay and lost local information
Only its ability to impose a common rule
Only local knowledge, excluding cross-branch effects
Manager counts rather than controlled decisions
fields.feedback: Neither central nor local authority is always superior. Compare information and incentive effects.

fields.q: A manager knows a customer needs an immediate service fix; headquarters lacks that detail. Which design uses the information with accountability?
options: Allow bounded local remedies with outcome review
Require every minor remedy to await uninformed central approval
Delegate remedies and remove reporting of consequences
Collect information but forbid local action regardless of delay
fields.feedback: Bounded delegation uses timely local information; review and incentives remain relevant.

fields.q: A manager postpones necessary maintenance to raise a current bonus, causing larger future repairs. Which remedy fits?
options: Include verified maintenance and longer-horizon value in evaluation
Raise the same current-profit bonus
Treat every postponement as efficient regardless of later damage
Judge only current cash spending and ignore asset condition
fields.feedback: The agent shifts costs beyond the reward horizon. Include later consequences.

fields.q: A policy adds $28,000 to one division’s profit and reduces another’s by $45,000. Other effects equal, what should headquarters see?
options: A $17,000 company loss
A $28,000 company gain
A $45,000 company loss
A $73,000 company gain
fields.feedback: 28,000−45,000=−17,000. Both incremental effects count.

fields.q: Seller opportunity cost is $18 and buyer net value is $30. At a $35 internal price the buyer refuses. What was missed?
options: The $12 company gain differs from the buyer’s −$5 margin
The company loses $5 because the charge is a resource cost
The buyer must accept whenever the seller gains
The company gains $17 because seller margin is company value
fields.feedback: Company value is 30−18=12; buyer margin is 30−35=−5. The accounting price can block real gains.

fields.q: A profit center raises margin by moving service work to an uncharged shared unit. Company resource use rises. What is the issue?
options: Local profit omits attributable costs imposed elsewhere
A reported profit center cannot cause company losses
The unit became a cost center when work moved
The move is harmless when another unit receives the invoice
fields.feedback: Local profit can omit costs caused in other units; include shared effects.

fields.q: A support unit saves $9,000 by cutting checks, creating $24,000 downstream losses. Which evaluation fits?
options: A $15,000 company loss; service effects must accompany cost control
A $9,000 gain because the unit met its target
A $24,000 loss because savings do not count
A $33,000 gain because both effects are internal
fields.feedback: 9,000−24,000=−15,000. Evaluate the service value alongside costs.

fields.q: Shared engineers provide valuable expertise, but marketing changes specifications without consultation. Which response preserves the benefit and fixes the weakness?
options: Keep shared expertise and coordinate specification changes
Duplicate every engineer by product without comparing costs
Reward department activity counts and omit launch outcomes
Eliminate marketing input to avoid coordination
fields.feedback: Functional expertise and cross-functional coordination can coexist. A coordination problem need not justify abandoning shared specialists.

fields.q: A custom order needs scarce capacity. Operations knows which work would be displaced; sales knows customer value. Which process fits?
options: Share displaced contribution before accepting the promise
Accept whenever revenue exceeds material cost
Report only operations spending after acceptance
Raise separate sales and cost targets without sharing capacity
fields.feedback: Acceptance requires contribution and production opportunity cost before commitment.

fields.q: Product divisions have profit responsibility, but one harms a shared brand. What should headquarters retain?
options: Shared-brand coordination alongside local accountability
Only separate scores because each includes all brand effects
No measures because spillovers make evaluation impossible
Direct approval of every minor task as the only solution
fields.feedback: M-form does not eliminate shared assets or spillovers.

fields.q: A manager expects strong demand but forecasts low because bonuses reward beating the forecast. Which change targets this?
options: Separate forecasts from negotiable bonus hurdles and verify demand evidence
Raise the same bonus for beating the submitted forecast
Treat every unexpected demand shock as fraud
Approve forecasts without comparing evidence
fields.feedback: The target rewards understatement; strengthen truthful planning rather than easy-hurdle rewards.

fields.q: Carryover stops unnecessary December spending, but managers may overstate future needs. Which complementary control fits?
options: Review credible need and service evidence before releasing carried funds
Treat carryover as proof of truthful requests
Spend all carried funds immediately to avoid review
Remove service measures because expenditure is observable
fields.feedback: Carryover fixes one incentive while private needs information remains. Review addresses the remaining slack margin.
